intro.html: Groups agree and disagree in many different ways. A vote can be unanimous or face a lone dissent; a family can live in accord or in discord; a quarrel can be polite or acrimonious. Several of these words are built from the same Latin pieces: sent (feel, think), cord (heart) and con- (together) against dis- (apart).

Coming together: consensus (general agreement), unanimous (everyone agrees), concur (to agree), accord (harmony), coalesce (to merge into one). Pulling apart: dissent (disagreement with the majority), discord (lack of harmony), acrimonious (bitter), divisive (splitting people), controversy (a long public dispute).

words.ex: After a long debate, the club reached a {consensus}: pizza on Fridays.
words.ctx: The scientists had argued for years, but a {consensus} slowly formed: nearly all of them came to accept that the bones belonged to a new species.
words.etym: From Latin consensus, “agreement,” from consentire: con (together) + sentire (to feel, to think).
words.note: Consensus already means general agreement, so “general consensus” says the same thing twice.

mn.cue: CON-SENSE-us: we all SENSE the same
mn.text: The class votes on a name for the new bunny, and almost every hand goes up for “Clover.” When nearly everyone senses the same, the group has a {consensus}.

scene.alt: Children raise their hands together to agree on a name for the class bunny.

words.ex: The vote was {unanimous}: all twelve players wanted the blue jerseys.
words.ctx: Usually the judges argue for hours, but this year their decision was {unanimous}; every one of them chose the same cherry pie as the winner.
words.etym: From Latin unanimus, “of one mind”: unus (one) + animus (mind).

mn.text: Nana Mae, Nana Lou and Grandpa Gus judge the pie contest, and all three hold up a perfect 10 for the cherry pie. Every vote the same: the decision is {unanimous}.

scene.alt: Three grandparent judges all hold up a score of 10 for a cherry pie.

words.ex: Both coaches {concurred} that the game should wait until the storm passed.
words.ctx: I thought the movie was far too long, and my sister {concurred}; she had fallen asleep twice before the ending.
words.etym: From Latin concurrere, “to run together”: con (together) + currere (to run).

mn.text: Two dogs spot the same ball and race for it side by side, of one mind. When two people’s thoughts run together like that, they {concur}.

scene.alt: Two dogs run side by side toward the same ball on the beach.

words.ex: The neighbors reached an {accord} about where to build the shared fence.
words.ctx: For years the two villages quarreled over the river, but the new {accord} let each draw water on alternate days, and the arguments finally stopped.
words.etym: From Latin ad (to) + cor, cordis (heart): hearts brought together.
words.note: Of your own accord means freely, without being asked: “She cleaned her room of her own accord.”

mn.text: Lin plays three notes at once on the piano, and they sound lovely together: a chord. People who get along in harmony like that are in {accord}.

scene.alt: A woman plays a pleasant chord on the piano while a couple listens happily.

words.def: to come together to form one whole
words.ex: Tiny raindrops {coalesced} into one fat drop at the edge of the roof.
words.ctx: At first the volunteers worked in scattered groups, but over the summer they {coalesced} into one well-organized team with a single plan.
words.etym: From Latin coalescere, “to grow together”: co (together) + alescere (to grow up).

mn.text: Dozens of little fish swim closer and closer until they move like one big fish. When separate parts join into a single whole, they {coalesce}.

scene.alt: Many small fish swim close together to form one big fish shape, and two more join them.

words.def: disagreement with an official or majority view
words.ex: Only one hand went up in {dissent} when the class voted for the zoo trip.
words.ctx: The proposal passed easily, but not without {dissent}: two members of the committee wrote a long letter explaining why they thought it was a mistake.
words.etym: From Latin dissentire, “to differ in feeling”: dis (apart) + sentire (to feel, to think).
words.note: Dissent (disagreement) sounds just like descent (a way down).

mn.cue: DIS-SENT: one vote SENT the other way
mn.text: Every hand goes up for the new rule except Marcus’s; he sends his vote the other way and says why. His “no” is a {dissent}.

scene.alt: At a meeting, three people raise their hands in favor while one man crosses his arms and votes no.

words.ex: A quarrel over the last pancake brought {discord} to the breakfast table.
words.ctx: The band sounded wonderful in rehearsal, but {discord} among its members, who argued over every song, broke it up before its first concert.
words.etym: From Latin discordia, from discors, “disagreeing”: dis (apart) + cor (heart).

mn.text: Kai strums one song on the guitar while Lila plays a different one on the violin, and the dog howls. Sounds that clash, like people who clash, are in {discord}.

scene.alt: A boy with a guitar and a girl with a violin play different tunes while a dog howls between them.

words.ex: The {acrimonious} argument over the parking space lasted twenty minutes.
words.ctx: What began as a friendly debate about the town fountain turned {acrimonious}: neighbors shouted, slammed doors and stopped speaking to each other for weeks.
words.etym: From acrimony, Latin acrimonia, “sharpness,” from acer, sharp, sour.

mn.cue: ACRI = ACID: a sour, bitter fight
mn.text: The two lemonade sellers argue over the best corner until their words turn as sour as acid. Their quarrel is {acrimonious}.

scene.alt: Two lemonade sellers point and shout bitterly at each other.

words.def: causing disagreement or splitting people into sides
words.ex: Pineapple on pizza is a surprisingly {divisive} topic in our family.
words.ctx: The plan to close the old library proved {divisive}, splitting the town into two angry camps that argued about it at every meeting.
words.etym: From Latin divisus, “divided,” from dividere, “to divide.”

mn.text: Put a pineapple pizza on the table, and the family splits in two: half cheer, half groan. A topic that divides people is {divisive}.

scene.alt: A pineapple pizza splits a table: one man cheers, a woman recoils.

words.ex: The new school mascot stirred up a {controversy} on the letters page of the local paper.
words.ctx: The painting caused a {controversy} when it was unveiled: some critics called it a masterpiece, others called it a mess, and the arguments filled the papers for months.
words.etym: From Latin controversia, “a dispute,” from controversus, “turned against”: contra (against) + versus (turned).

mn.text: At the museum, half the crowd loves the new painting and half calls it a mess, and the argument goes on for weeks in public. Views turned against each other make a {controversy}.

scene.alt: Two museum visitors hold up opposite signs, love and mess, on either side of a new painting.

head: root
with con- or ac- (together)
with dis- (apart)
after.cap: Same root, opposite prefixes, opposite meanings.

after.html: Two more are built the same way: unanimous is un (one) + anim (mind): of one mind. Concur is con (together) + cur (run): minds that run together.
Consensus already means general agreement, so “general consensus” is padding; just say consensus. And dissent (disagreement) is not descent (a way down): dis + sent, to feel apart.

items.q: The jury voted 11 to 1. Was the verdict unanimous?
items.why: Unanimous means everyone agrees, every single vote. Eleven out of twelve is a strong majority, not a unanimous vote.

items.q: Which sentence uses the right word?
choices: The judge wrote a strong dissent from the majority opinion.
The hikers began their dissent from the summit at noon.
The plane made a slow dissent toward the runway.
items.why: Dissent is disagreement. A way down is spelled descent.

items.q: Which phrase is wordy because it repeats an idea?
items.why: Consensus already means general agreement, so “general consensus” says it twice.

items.q: The split between the two business partners was acrimonious. What was it like?
items.why: Acrimonious means bitter and angry, from Latin acer, sharp or sour.
